extracted.intended_audience: journalists and content creators covering disability
extracted.subtask_description: Practical guidance and standards for journalists and content creators to report on disability accurately, respectfully, accessibly, and ethically — covering interviewing, language, visuals, investigation, and digital accessibility. The page aggregates tip sheets, toolkits, and guidelines intended to shape newsroom practice and content production.

rubrics_metrics.name: Interview preparation and follow-up (before, during, after)
rubrics_metrics.description: What reporters should do before, during and after interviewing someone with a disability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Includes practical steps to prepare, conduct, and follow up on interviews with disabled people (see NCDJ video 'Disability Reporting 101'). Emphasizes preparation, respectful conduct during interviews, and appropriate follow-up practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid 'inspiration porn'
rubrics_metrics.description: How journalists can avoid so-called 'inspiration porn.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not frame disabled people primarily as objects of inspiration for nondisabled audiences. See Columbia Journalism Review advice and Stella Young's TED talk 'I'm not your inspiration, thank you very much' for examples and discussion of the harm of inspirational framing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Report with care on disability
rubrics_metrics.description: Practice careful, informed reporting when covering disability topics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Follow guidance such as Amanda Morris's 'How to Report With Care on Disability' — prioritize accuracy, dignity, context, and centering disabled voices when covering disability-related stories.

rubrics_metrics.name: Ensure fair coverage of disability
rubrics_metrics.description: Editorial teams should ensure fair coverage of disability.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: UNESCO-produced practical manual and master class provide hands-on advice for newsrooms to audit and change editorial processes to produce fair, non-stereotyped coverage of disability.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use a reporting checklist for disability stories
rubrics_metrics.description: Ask important questions as you write and report a story about disability (Reporting on Disability: A Checklist).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the NCDJ checklist to self-audit stories — includes questions about sources, context, framing, language, and accessibility. Designed as a pre-publication checklist for reporters and editors.

rubrics_metrics.name: Investigate disability issues and understand relevant laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand federal disability laws and methods for investigative reporting on disability issues.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NCDJ tip sheet and Global Investigative Journalism Network guide explain key legal frameworks, data sources, and investigative approaches reporters should use when investigating disability-related issues.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use specialized guidance for vision/blindness coverage
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow resources tailored to reporting about blindness and vision loss.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: American Foundation for the Blind's comprehensive guide includes interviewing advice and reporting tips specific to blindness and vision-loss communities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ableist tropes (e.g., the 'pity trap')
rubrics_metrics.description: When covering disability, avoid ableist tropes like the 'pity trap'.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NPR and other guides discuss common tropes (pity, heroification, sensationalism) to avoid and offer alternative framing that respects agency and context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choose appropriate identity-first vs. person-first language
rubrics_metrics.description: Understand the distinction between identity-first and person-first language and use the form preferred by the person/community.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Association of Health Care Journalists and other resources discuss when to use identity-first (e.g., 'autistic person') versus person-first ('person with autism') language and emphasize asking individuals/community preference and being consistent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use accurate, neutral, objective language
rubrics_metrics.description: Portray individuals with disabilities using language that is accurate, neutral and objective.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ADA National Network factsheet and other style guides recommend avoiding sensationalist, dehumanizing, or value-laden terms; prioritize clarity and neutrality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use plain language for accessibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt plain language: common words, short sentences, clear structure to make content accessible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: ProPublica/Nieman Lab examples and the Plain Truth Project highlight techniques for simplifying prose to improve comprehension for people with intellectual and developmental disabilities and broader audiences.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consider intersectionality in reporting
rubrics_metrics.description: Language and intersectional reporting matter when covering disabilities — consider race, gender, socioeconomic status, geography, etc.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guides such as NBCU Academy and others stress that disability intersects with other identities and reporters should include that context in coverage rather than treating disability in isolation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use specialized language guidance for mental and behavioral health
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow recommendations about language when reporting on mental and behavioral health conditions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Carter Center and the American Psychiatric Association provide specific suggestions for respectful, accurate language and context when covering mental health topics.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create inclusive and accessible interview settings
rubrics_metrics.description: Design interview environments that are accessible and inclusive for people with disabilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: University of Vermont Center on Disability and Community Inclusion and other guides offer practical tips for physical accessibility, scheduling, communication accommodations, and other logistics to make interviews accessible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow etiquette when a sign language interpreter is present
rubrics_metrics.description: Use proper interview etiquette when a sign language interpreter is present.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Gallaudet University tips explain positioning, addressing the interviewee directly, pacing, and other best practices when working with interpreters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portray people with disabilities authentically in visuals
rubrics_metrics.description: Use visuals that authentically portray individuals with disabilities rather than stereotyped images.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Getty Images' Disability Collection and Shutterstock/WID 'Authentic Portrayals' guide provide examples and guidance for selecting photographs and footage that reflect real lives, contexts, and diversity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid stereotypical visual representations
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid stock photography and visuals that rely on stereotypical representations of disabled people.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Articles and resources discuss common visual stereotypes to avoid (e.g., overuse of assistive devices as shorthand, pitying expressions) and how to source or commission more authentic imagery.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use film and television toolkits for accurate representation
rubrics_metrics.description: Apply toolkits for representing disabilities in film, television, and documentary work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: GADIM, FWD-Doc, Doc Society and related toolkits offer production-level suggestions for casting, consulting, narrative framing, accessibility on set, and inclusion practices in screen media.

rubrics_metrics.name: Apply accessible graphic design principles
rubrics_metrics.description: Make graphic design accessible to people with disabilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The 'Access-ability' handbook provides design-level guidance (contrast, typography, layout, labelling) to help graphic designers produce accessible visual materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Make news websites and digital content accessible (follow W3C standards)
rubrics_metrics.description: Follow web accessibility standards and take steps to make news websites accessible to all audiences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Nieman Reports, NCAM resources, and the W3C 'Making the Web Accessible' collection outline technical standards (e.g., WCAG), implementation steps, and newsroom workflows to improve web accessibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Create accessible social media content
rubrics_metrics.description: Produce social media content that is accessible to people with disabilities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disability:IN and other guides provide platform-specific tips (alt text, captions, formatting) to ensure social posts are usable by screen reader users and those who need captions or simplified layouts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Publish accessible content and dissemination practices
rubrics_metrics.description: Adopt publishing practices that ensure content is accessible (including distribution and marketing).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: NCDJ and 'Accessible Social Media' resources list tips for website accessibility, file formats, captioning, dissemination practices, and marketing content that is disability-friendly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Follow curated toolkits and living documents (use community feedback)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use living toolkits and resources that are open for community comments to continuously improve disability coverage.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Donald W. Reynolds Journalism Institute toolkit and similar living documents encourage newsrooms to use, adapt, and accept feedback from disability communities to improve coverage over time.
